Neonatal Amazonian motmots emerge from calcareous eggs at a remarkably modest body mass of 12.05 grams [Wwb = 12.05 grams], a value consistent with the altricial developmental mode characteristic of coraciiform birds. This initial weight stands in stark contrast to the substantial adult dimensions the nestlings will ultimately attain. During the incubation period, which requires a consistent thermal environment, the developing embryo progresses through organogenesis within the albumen-buffered egg. Field records indicate that the incubation period, measured at a cavity temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], results in hatching after approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days]. This duration is relatively brief for a bird of this ultimate size and likely reflects the intense predation pressure typical of Neotropical rainforest understories, where prolonged exposure in the nest cavity would elevate mortality risk. The newly hatched chick is entirely dependent on bi-parental provisioning, with both adults contributing to brooding and feeding duties during the early nestling phase. The rapid growth trajectory that follows is fueled by a diet predominantly composed of large arthropods and small vertebrates, which the parents deliver at frequent intervals throughout the day.

As the developing chick progresses through the pin-feathered nestling stage, a critical developmental milestone is the achievement of fledging. Under the stable thermal conditions provided by the nest cavity, which we recorded at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], young motmots typically depart the nest at 30.5 days after hatching [tx = 30.5 days after hatching]. This fledging age is intermediate among the Momotidae; it is shorter than that observed in larger-bodied congeners but somewhat prolonged relative to smaller-bodied species within the order Coraciiformes. The post-fledging period is particularly hazardous for the juvenile bird, which must rapidly acquire foraging skills while still receiving occasional provisioning from the adults. During this phase, the young motmot exhibits a distinctive tail-wagging display believed to function as a signal of submission or perhaps an anti-predator mechanism. The nutritional independence that follows the fledging period marks the onset of the juvenile stage, a phase characterized by extensive dispersal and exploration of the complex forest matrix.

Sexual maturation in the Amazonian motmot does not occur immediately upon reaching adult body size; rather, it follows a more protracted schedule. Respirometry measurements obtained from captive individuals at a body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C] indicate that puberty is attained at 91.5 days after hatching [tp = 91.5 days after hatching]. This timing suggests that gonadal activation is delayed until well after the fledgling has achieved full nutritional independence and has developed the necessary foraging proficiency to support the energetic demands of future reproduction. The onset of gametogenesis is likely cued by a combination of endogenous developmental programs and external environmental signals, including photoperiod and food availability. It is noteworthy that this age at puberty is considerably shorter than the age at first successful reproduction, a pattern commonly observed in long-lived tropical bird species where territory acquisition and pair formation impose additional delays on breeding commencement. The young bird first attains the definitive adult plumage during this period, becoming indistinguishable from mature individuals in the field.

The onset of first breeding in the Amazonian motmot is deferred considerably beyond the point of sexual maturation. This modest annual reproductive output is characteristic of a slow life-history strategy, where adult survival is prioritized over high fecundity. The delay in first reproduction allows young birds to accumulate experience in foraging and territory defense, presumably enhancing their future breeding success and long-term fitness. The resulting daily reproduction rate is approximately 0.013 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.013 eggs per day].

The Amazonian motmot exhibits a substantial degree of sexual size dimorphism in its ultimate adult body mass. Adult females attain a maximum wet weight of 102 grams [Wwi = 102 grams], whereas males are appreciably heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 112 grams [Wwi = 112 grams]. This difference is thought to relate to sexual selection on male body size, possibly linked to competition for nesting cavities or display sites.
